title: Combinatorics and graph theory
audience: a college student in a mathematics degree program (or a related major such as physics, computer science or economics), or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn to count and to reason about networks: counting principles, binomial coefficients and combinatorial proofs, inclusion–exclusion, the pigeonhole principle and Ramsey numbers, recurrence relations and generating functions, graphs and isomorphism, trees and spanning trees, connectivity, Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths, matchings and Hall's theorem, coloring and planarity, and network flows, with algorithms in Python.
primary_reading: Applied Combinatorics by Mitchel T. Keller and William T. Trotter (free online)

weeks.4: The pigeonhole principle and Ramsey numbers
weeks.8: Trees, spanning trees and counting trees
weeks.12: Network flows and the max-flow min-cut theorem

blocks.deliverable: Prove two identities by double counting.
Count derangements and surjections with inclusion–exclusion.
Solve a supplied recurrence with a generating function and check it in code.
Week 7 midterm; implement a minimum spanning tree algorithm.
Find a maximum matching and prove that it is maximum.
Compute a maximum flow and a minimum cut of equal capacity.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Discrete structures report: implement and test in plain Python a solver for linear recurrences, breadth-first search, Kruskal's and Dijkstra's algorithms, a bipartite matching algorithm and a maximum-flow algorithm, prove two of them correct, and apply them to a supplied scheduling and assignment problem in a written report.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
